outcomes: An application composes plugins, child modules, dependency providers, and shutdown hooks under one lifecycle owner
Build-time generation produces every artifact a packaged workload needs without opening a runtime resource
A failed startup releases exactly what it acquired and reports the failure to its caller instead of ending the host process
A stop signal drains the application on the framework's own deadline instead of waiting to be killed
nonGoals: Restarting a failed plugin or supervising a crashed process
Generating code, routes, or manifests while the application is running
Promising that a pre-1.0 minor release keeps the previous lifecycle contract

requirements.text: start() warms plugins up sequentially in module-tree order, collects migration sources, builds the dependency container, runs migrate hooks, starts plugins concurrently, and only then runs the application runner.
generate() and postGenerate() run only from build(); postGenerate observes every artifact the generate barrier produced, and start() never invokes generate().
build() invalidates the capability manifest before generation and writes it only after generation succeeds, so a failed build leaves no manifest that appears to describe it.
Registering a provider or mounting a module after the container context was first read rebuilds that context, so the started application contains every declared registration.
A module requirement that no visible provider satisfies fails when the container is composed, not when the missing dependency is first resolved.
stop() runs shutdown hooks in reverse registration order, stops plugins in reverse module-tree order, closes the container last, and does nothing when the application is not running.

A startup failure stops only the plugins whose start() resolved, closes the container, leaves the application not running, and re-throws to the caller; every additional concurrent start failure is logged rather than discarded.

bootstrapServe builds the application inside its failure guard and reports a construction-time or start-time failure as exactly one structured log line before exiting non-zero, never logging the same failure twice.
SIGTERM and SIGINT drive one graceful stop per process, exit zero only when the drain resolves, exit non-zero when it rejects, and force-exit non-zero once the shutdown deadline elapses.

A TypeScript workload enforces a Domain Access & Replication Contract from the declaration itself: construction applies the architecture protocol's own verdict, and every read, write, rebuild, and deletion follows the declared freshness bound, ordering, late-event, single-writer, and deletion rules. Neither runtime is its own oracle: Go and TypeScript answer one shared conformance corpus, so a behavior that differs between them fails on one side instead of shipping as two runtimes.

A component that enforces a contract contributes one capability-manifest row carrying the declared contract verbatim, under the identity and provenance every other contribution carries. The row is evidence and never authority: emitting it cannot create a cross-domain permission, only a reviewed manifest edit can. A project that enforces nothing emits no rows, and the bytes TypeScript emits are the bytes the Go detector reads back.

Every api() plugin that scans a route folder (a scanPath or autoScan on), every StaticPlugin without skipLoading, and every events() plugin that scans a handler folder exports its generated loader under its own key: <family>-loader for the first in module-tree registration order, <family>-<n>-loader for the others. The packaged entrypoint registers each key and each plugin resolves only its own, so a packaged workload serves every instance. A plugin that owns no loader resolves none.
